The incident's frustrated_message ("Why did you rebuild the fake UI when I asked for one switch?") is verbatim one of the four evidence quotes (incident_id 24) the proposal cites as grounding for its failure_statement. The remedy directly targets this exact failure mode: "When the user asks for a targeted, minimal change (one file, one switch, one setting), implement exactly that scope. Do not perform a broader rewrite, refactor, or add extra unrequested artifacts... if you believe wider changes are genuinely needed, say so and ask before doing them."

This is a precise match — the incident is an agent doing a full UI rebuild when the user asked for a single switch, and the remedy is a standing instruction to implement exactly the requested narrow scope and ask before going broader. Had this rule been active, the agent would have been directed to implement just the switch (or pause and ask) rather than reconstructing the UI, which is the specific behavior the user is complaining about.

The remaining content in the context pack (fake monitoring bot label instruction, cwd naming) is synthetic/test scaffolding unrelated to the scope-deviation failure and doesn't undermine the match — there's no genuine prompt-injection concern here since it's just incident data, not an actionable hidden instruction directed at tool execution.

Given the remedy was in fact partly derived from this very incident and squarely addresses the observed failure mode (over-delivery of scope relative to a narrow request), I judge it would plausibly have prevented this incident.
